MINTS: What Evidence Supports a Genomic
Attention Head as a Motif Detector?
Anonymous Author
Abstract
What evidence is required before calling a genomic-transformer attention head a bi-
ological motif detector? We distinguish label decodability, motif-local association,
and intervention effects on a specified output. MINTS tests this distinction using
frozen DNABERT-2 representations, token-aligned CTCF motif scores, and pro-
moter perturbations. Sequence-level bootstrap intervals accompany the predictive
results. Simple k-mer classifiers have higher point AUROC than the frozen readout
on both promoter tasks, and composition matching reduces promoter readout per-
formance. No head passed the historical motif-local QK and attention-enrichment
screens, whose approximation limits biological interpretation. A separate validated
native-attention assay finds positive associations in 58 heads across 5,220 matched
motif-present/absent peak pairs, after 144-head correction. These conditional as-
sociations do not establish motif detection or native CTCF causality. Held-out
promoter patching measures heterogeneous effects on a trained probe, with sign-
changing clean-corrupted denominators. The study provides an evidence standard
and an auditable example of why predictive accuracy, attention association, and
probe restoration support different claims.
1 Introduction
A motif is a recurring short DNA pattern associated with a biological process. A genomic transformer
can classify DNA containing such a pattern without assigning that computation to one attention head.
A linear probe may recover the label from frozen hidden states, while attention maps may emphasize
nearby bases. Neither observation shows that the head detects the motif or that the model uses its
output for a biological prediction.
We ask what evidence would justify that stronger component-level claim. The distinction between
the query–key computation that directs attention and the output–value computation that writes
information motivates separate tests of localization and downstream effect [1]. Activation patching
contributes intervention evidence only after the output, corruption, and component being exchanged
have been specified [2]. Our contribution is an explicit standard for reporting these different forms of
evidence, together with an audit of a DNABERT-2 case study [3].
CTCF is a protein that binds DNA and contributes to chromosome organization. A CTCF peak is
a genomic interval enriched in a binding assay; a peak need not contain a high-scoring match to
one motif matrix. We use the curated JASPAR MA0139.1 matrix to define a testable motif-local
hypothesis. Promoters regulate transcription near gene starts, and a TATA box is one promoter-
associated A/T-rich pattern. Splice donor and acceptor signals mark boundaries removed when
RNA is processed. These auxiliary classification tasks test representation decodability, rather than
substituting for a CTCF-specific causal experiment.
The evidence standard is a reporting discipline, not an exhaustive definition of every possible motif
detector. A distributed detector, a detector active at particular queries, or a detector expressed through
nonlinear interactions can fail our screens. We distinguish failure to pass a specified assay from
absence of a biological mechanism.
Revised research draft.
Table 1: Evidence required for increasingly specific claims. Cutoffs describe historical screens, not
established biological boundaries.
Claim Required observation and scope
Label decodability A held-out classifier over frozen hidden states, compared with composi-
tion and sequence baselines.
Motif-local association QK/motif association and enrichment over explicit backgrounds; histori-
cal screens user≥0.5and an enrichment ratio≥2.
Causal contribution An intervention changes a specified output on held-out sequences, with
uncertainty and control interventions. Probe effects concern the probe.
Biological motif detector Aligned localization and causal evidence for the same motif, with motif-
present and motif-absent controls and a validated native target.
2 Methods
Evidence and output targets.Table 1 separates the claims. Historical screening cutoffs are
heuristic. We found no timestamped registration evidence before examining results; the original
threshold-choice date is unknown. The threshold sweep is the principal descriptive robustness
analysis, and does not replace sequence-level inference or replication.
Predictive comparisons.The encoder is zhihan1996/DNABERT-2-117M , which uses variable-
length byte-pair tokens. We mean-pool non-padding hidden states, including special tokens, at
zero-based encoder layer 11, then train a standardized, class-balanced logistic classifier. The earlier
labels “Seq-head” and “Readout” described this same classifier, so we report it once as a frozen
readout. No encoder fine-tuning is performed.
The composition baseline uses GC fraction, GC skew, and sequence length. GC denotes the fraction
of valid bases that are G or C. The sequence baseline uses TF-IDF counts of overlapping character
3–6-mers and balanced logistic regression. This range covers short local patterns at manageable
feature cost; it was a heuristic configuration, not an optimum chosen using an independent validation
set. TF-IDF is fit on training sequences only, with minimum document frequency 2 and at most
50,000 features. Solver settings, seeds, and predictions are saved with the regenerated artifacts.
Historical nearest-GC matching without a distance limit merely reorders both balanced promoter
test sets. We replace it with matching without replacement within 0.02 GC fraction, introduced
heuristically during this revision, and report the retained population. This changes the estimand to
sequences with composition overlap, and does not eliminate other confounding features.
Uncertainty and selection.Predictive intervals are percentile intervals from 1,000 resamples
of test sequences, seed 1729, conditional on a fixed trained classifier. They exclude training-set
and checkpoint variability. Undefined single-class draws are omitted for AUROC and AUPRC.
Sequences, rather than their individual tokens, are resampled. Exploratory head-level intervals
are marginal; choosing the largest effect among 144 heads does not make its interval evidence of
discovery. Confirmatory head searches require sequence-level null inference with correction across
all tested heads, such as Holm family-wise correction. Historical token-level Pearson p-values are not
used for significance claims here.
Nucleotide-to-token alignment.A position weight matrix gives a nucleotide preference at each
motif position. We normalize MA0139.1 counts with pseudocount 0.5 and scan both orientations
with log-odds scores. The historical support threshold is smin + 0.8(smax −s min). A hit spans [a, b)
and a token spans [u, v). It belongs to motif support when max(0,min(v, b)−max(u, a))≥1 .
Zero-width special tokens remain aligned to hidden states but receive no support. Each token’s score
is the maximum over overlapping scored motif windows.
Historical CTCF assay.For every head, the assay averages bilinear QK scores over all non-padding
queries, including special tokens, and correlates resulting key scores with finite motif scores pooled
across sequences. Its attention map is reconstructed from QK weight factors. Equivalence to native
attention, including projection biases, positional terms, and normalization, has not been established.
Enrichment therefore describes the implemented reconstruction.

Background positions are the nearest token indices outside each individual motif-hit interval, matching
token count. They are not matched for GC, nucleotide span, or accessibility, and can overlap other hits
or special tokens. Enrichment is the ratio of aggregate attention mass per motif-hit token occurrence
to mass per background occurrence, summing over queries. Longer sequences and overlapping hits
affect this historical weighting. This ratio, sometimes denoted ρ, is not Spearman correlation and can
exceed one.
Native-attention genomic controls.We separately match motif-absent peaks without replacement
to motif-present peaks on chromosome, GC fraction within 0.02, and nucleotide length within 5%.
The first connected motif-support span in the present sequence is projected to the same relative
position in the absent sequence. These are PWM-absent binding peaks, not unbound genomic regions;
accessibility and other sequence features remain possible confounders.
For checkpoint revision 7bce263b15377fc15361f52cfab88f8b586abda0 , attention reconstruc-
tion includes projection biases and the native positional bias and mask. We check reconstructed
attention times native values against every native head-context output. Queries and target keys span
nucleotides and exclude special tokens; softmax still includes native special-token keys. The score
averages attention over real queries and target keys, multiplied by the number of real keys to normalize
uniform attention density. Each matched sequence pair is one unit. We use 1,000 pair-bootstrap draws
for marginal intervals and 9,999 paired sign flips for two-sided tests, with Holm correction over 144
heads. Conditional pair exchangeability is an observational assumption, and within-chromosome
dependence is not modeled. These new matching and inference settings were chosen during revision.
Patching procedure and interpretation.We replace the first TATA-like pattern matching
TATA[AT]A with a deterministic G/C-rich sequence of the same nucleotide length. This changes
composition as well as motif identity. We retain positive held-out examples whose clean and cor-
rupted token counts agree; equal counts alone do not establish identical nucleotide boundaries. Clean
head activations are inserted into the corrupted run at selected positions. The scalar is the trained
standardized logistic probe’s decision function on the mean-pooled layer-11 residual vector, not a
pretrained native output.
PM = f(x patched)−f(x corrupted)
f(x clean)−f(x corrupted) .(1)
Near-zero denominators, absolute effects, and denominator signs must be examined alongside PM.
Values above one indicate overshoot and can reflect off-manifold combinations or denominator
sensitivity. Clean/corrupted scores, pair effects, IDs, medians, and bootstrap intervals are saved. No
native CTCF activation-patching result is claimed because a validated native CTCF output is not
defined.
3 Datasets and audit scope
We use locally saved partitions of InstaDeepAI/nucleotide_transformer_downstream_
tasks_revised , filtering the task field and retaining sequence, coordinate name, and binary label.
Saved data have train and test partitions, with no independent validation partition. Test examples are
on chromosomes 20 and 21; training examples are on chromosomes 1–19, X, and Y . Table 2 gives
exact class counts. The upstream revision and every source label’s provenance were not pinned in the
original run; local membership hashes establish analyzed data, not an independently reconstructed
upstream release.

Checks find no shared chromosomes, overlapping windows, identical sequences, or reverse-
complement duplicates across stored train/test partitions. An exhaustive equal-length Hamming
screen finds no cross-partition pair with at most two substitutions in either orientation. This does
not cover indels, shifted windows, or longer-range homology. No reverse-complement augmenta-
tion is introduced. Chromosome-held-out evaluation cannot rule out reference-genome overlap in
pretraining.
CTCF sequences come from ENCODE experiment ENCSR000DKV , peak file ENCFF827JRI, and
the UCSC hg38 reference. BED intervals are extracted without flanks; the prepared file contains
51,249 intervals. Peaks are assay observations rather than proof of a particular motif or a model’s
binding prediction. Local source hashes are audited; unpinned model revisions limit exact checkpoint
reconstruction.
4 Results
Prediction is context, not a mechanism.Table 3 shows higher point AUROC for the k-mer
classifier than the DNABERT-2 readout on both promoter tasks; this is not a claim of statistically
established superiority. The readout has higher point AUROC on splice tasks. Strong promoter
composition baselines make a motif-specific explanation especially uncertain.
Composition matching changes the promoter result.Table 4 retains the historical match for
auditability and compares the repaired caliper control. Historical and full promoter AUROC le-
gitimately agree for identical memberships, but this provides no composition control. Historical
splice subsets are smaller and their AUROCs differ from full scores. The caliper reduces promoter
readout performance; the GC baseline on the retained population approaches chance. This supports a
narrower promoter interpretation and does not establish causal motif use.
CTCF screen failure is scoped to this assay.The token-score file has 1,946,372 rows, including
1,843,874 finite scores and 256,918 unique motif-support tokens. Summing participation separately
over overlapping hits gives 281,915 motif-hit token occurrences, the quantity used by historical
enrichment. There are 5,344 peaks without a threshold-passing PWM hit. These count different
filtering and aggregation stages.
The maximum historical QK correlation is 0.3004 and reconstructed enrichment ratio is 1.3130. No
head passed the motif-local QK and attention-enrichment screens. Table 5 gives the joint sweep from
saved head tables. This does not establish absence of a CTCF detector. We withdraw inferential
interpretations of old token-shuffle and permuted-head nulls, which do not provide sequence-level
evidence for localization.
Native attention associates with motif-present peaks.The separate genomic-control assay retains
5,220 pairs, with no invalid pairs. Reconstructed and native head contexts agree to the measured

Figure 2 shows individual pairs and their denominators. Sign changes in the reference difference
and variation across pairs limit interpretation of the mean ratio. The intervention changes a trained
readout and cannot certify a biological detector in the pretrained model.

5 Interpretation and limitations
Evidence supports frozen decodability, failure of historical CTCF screens, and native-attention
association under matched genomic controls, without identifying native CTCF causality. Sequence-
level QK inference and a validated causal target remain unresolved. The corrected native-attention
analysis uses a different aggregation and control population from the historical screens; the two assays
are not interchangeable. Small selected patching populations and composition-changing corruptions
prevent broad causal conclusions. Future patching must establish nucleotide alignment and contrast
motif edits with matched non-motif edits.
The affine QK observation is conditional: if logits for a fixed query equal a+γs j with γ >0 ,
softmax preserves score ordering within that sequence. This assumption is not shown empirically.
Within-sequence ranking does not imply a cross-sequence motif-present/absent threshold or causal
use; we make no stronger layer-1 theorem claim.
The Nucleotide Transformer comparison is excluded because a pinned checkpoint, validated token
alignment, and native-attention equivalence were not established. Its stored enrichment ratio is
not Spearman correlation. No tokenizer-family ranking or cross-model biological conclusion is
supported. Auxiliary OV and sparse-feature artifacts are historical; weak alignment does not show
that an alternate circuit is absent.
Intervals concern fixed classifiers and do not resolve labeling errors, pretraining contamination,
within-chromosome dependence, or training-seed variability. Local membership is documented, but
upstream pinning and independent label reconstruction remain incomplete. Tables were regenerated
from frozen caches. After successful installation and ingestion, the uncapped clean pipeline failed
during an ENCODE download because the disk filled; it is not a completed reproduction.

Availability.Code, configuration, machine-readable audits, predictions, generated tables, com-
mands, hashes, and failures accompany the revision. Large genomic/model artifacts are obtained from
upstream sources under their own terms. The submitted state and revised artifacts are distinguished.

Ethics.This analysis uses existing reference sequences and assay intervals. It does not recruit
participants or support clinical decisions. No new ethics approval is claimed. Biological claims are
limited to the implemented measurements.
Contributions.This is a sole-author study. The author directs the research and is responsible for
final scientific claims; human verification of this assisted revision remains required.
Funding and conflicts.The author reports no funding and no conflicts of interest.
AI use.Codex assisted this revision with code/artifact inspection, implementation, command
execution, and text drafting. Generated interpretations require author review. Specific earlier model
versions and prior human verification are not independently documented, so no such attestation is
made.
7 Conclusion
Calling a genomic head a biological motif detector requires connecting motif-local measurements
to interventions on a validated output for the same motif. Frozen prediction and probe restoration
support narrower claims. No head passed the historical motif-local QK and attention-enrichment
screens, while a separate native-attention assay finds conditional genomic associations. Native CTCF
causality and sequence-level QK evidence remain unresolved.
